cards.t: The conduction system and the three pacemakers
q: what is the conduction system of the heart
why is the sinoatrial node the main pacemaker
what are the backup pacemakers and their rates
cards.x:
The conduction system is the heart's built-in wiring, and the impulse travels through it in a fixed order.

- It starts at the sinoatrial node, high in the right atrium just below the opening of the superior vena cava. This is the main pacemaker, firing 60 to 100 times per minute.
- The impulse then reaches the atrioventricular node at the junction of the atria and ventricles. This is the first backup pacemaker, at 40 to 60 per minute.
- From there it passes down the bundle of His, splits into the bundle branches, and spreads through the Purkinje network. This is the third pacemaker, at 20 to 40 per minute. It carries the impulse faster than any other conducting cell, so the ventricles work in sync.

Why doesn't every pacemaker fire at once? Natural hierarchy keeps the lower cells quiet, so the fastest one, the sinoatrial node, normally sets the rate. A lower pacemaker only takes over when the one above it fails. A nonconductive wall separates atria from ventricles, so in a normal heart the bundle of His is the only way across.

cards.t: Bachmann's bundle, the internodal tracts and the atrioventricular node
q: how does the impulse spread through the atria
what are the internodal tracts
what are the zones of the atrioventricular node
cards.x:
Once the sinoatrial node fires, the impulse has to cross both atria and reach the atrioventricular node. Bachmann's bundle carries it from the right atrium to the left atrium and is the main route between the two. Three internodal tracts (superior anterior, middle and inferior posterior) run from the sinoatrial node toward the atrioventricular node. The superior anterior one is the fast tract and the inferior posterior one is the slow tract.

In most people only the fast tract actually attaches to the atrioventricular node. The other two end within the right atrium. That detail matters later, when we get to reentry circuits.

The atrioventricular node itself sits near the coronary sinus and has three zones: transition, compact and trigger.

cards.t: The bundle branches and the left fascicles
q: what are the bundle branches
what are the three fascicles of the left bundle branch
how do the right and left bundle branches differ
cards.x:
Below the bundle of His the wiring splits in two. The right bundle branch is a much longer piece of tissue that enters the right ventricle and ends in the Purkinje network. The left bundle branch is a small piece that quickly divides into three fascicles, which are small branches:

- Left posterior: finger-like projections across the back of the left ventricle.
- Interventricular septal: depolarizes (fires) the septum, which is what produces the Q wave.
- Left anterior: ends in the Purkinje network.

So the left side branches early into three pieces, while the right side stays a single long cable.

cards.t: The four properties of cardiac cells
q: what are the four properties of cardiac cells
what does automaticity mean
what is the difference between excitability and conductivity
cards.x:
Heart cells can do four things, and each has its own name:

- Automaticity: making its own impulse without being told to.
- Excitability: responding when an impulse or stimulus arrives.
- Contractility: contracting.
- Conductivity: passing the impulse on from one heart muscle cell to the next.

Automaticity is why the heart has pacemakers at all. Lower cells could fire on their own, but the natural hierarchy of pacemaker function stops them, so the sinoatrial node, the fastest pacemaker, normally sets the rate.

cards.t: The four chambers and how the ventricles fill
q: how does blood flow through the heart chambers
how much of ventricular filling is passive
why do the atria matter when they stop contracting
cards.x:
The right atrium receives deoxygenated blood from the two venae cavae, and the right ventricle pumps it to the lungs. The left atrium receives oxygenated blood from the lungs, and the left ventricle pumps it into the aorta.

Here is the useful twist: 70 to 80 percent of ventricular filling is passive. Blood simply drains from atrium to ventricle without the atria having to squeeze. That means the atria contribute only the last slice of the filling. It becomes important later when the atria stop contracting in atrial fibrillation, because the ventricles still fill most of the way on their own.

cards.t: The cardiac action potential (phases 4, 0, 1, 2 and 3)
q: what are the phases of the cardiac action potential
what ions move in each phase
why does potassium leave the cell in repolarization
cards.x:
An action potential is the electrical change a heart cell goes through each time it fires. It runs through five phases in the order 4, 0, 1, 2, 3:

- Phase 4, rest: more potassium inside, sodium and calcium outside; the inside sits at -90 millivolts and the cell is ready to respond.
- Phase 0, upstroke (depolarization): fast sodium channels open and sodium rushes in, making the inside positive.
- Phase 1, the notch: sodium channels close and potassium channels reopen, giving a slight negative shift.
- Phase 2, plateau: calcium enters and causes contraction while the voltage holds level.
- Phase 3, rapid repolarization: calcium channels close and potassium flows out, returning the inside to -90 millivolts.

The key point is that repolarization is potassium leaving the cell. Positive charge going out makes the inside negative again.

cards.t: Absolute and relative refractory periods
q: what is the absolute refractory period
what is the relative refractory period
why is the relative refractory period dangerous
cards.x:
After a heart cell fires, it needs a short recovery before it can fire again. That recovery has two parts, and the peak of the T wave divides them.

The absolute refractory period comes first, typically lasting about 180 milliseconds after an action potential. The cell will not respond to another stimulus at all. On the tracing it runs from the start of the QRS (the main spike, ventricular firing) up to the peak of the T wave.

The relative refractory period comes next, during repolarization, over the downslope of the T wave. The cell will now respond to a second stimulus, but it is very fragile, so a stimulus landing here can trigger an arrhythmia (an abnormal rhythm).

cards.t: The heart's vector and why lead II is the rhythm lead
q: why is lead II used for rhythm interpretation
what is the heart's vector
which way does the impulse travel through the heart
cards.x:
The heart sits in the middle of the chest, in the space called the mediastinum. The true pathway of the electrical impulse through it runs left and down, toward the left foot. That overall direction is called the heart's vector, and a shift of it outside the normal range is abnormal.

Lead II has a perfect view of that vector, which is why it is the lead used for rhythm interpretation. When you read a rhythm strip, lead II is the standard view.

cards.t: The bipolar limb leads (I, II, III) and Einthoven's triangle
q: what are leads I, II and III
what is Einthoven's triangle
where are the positive and negative poles of the limb leads
cards.x:
Leads I, II and III are the bipolar limb leads. Bipolar means each lead needs a real positive electrode and a real negative electrode. Together they form Einthoven's triangle across both shoulders and the left leg.

- Lead I: positive at the left shoulder, negative at the right shoulder.
- Lead II: positive at the left foot, negative at the right shoulder.
- Lead III: positive at the left foot, negative at the left shoulder.

Think of each positive electrode as a camera: the lead shows you the heart's electrical activity from that camera's point of view. These three leads, plus the augmented leads, make up the first six leads of the 12-lead tracing and are used to find the axis.

cards.t: The augmented leads (aVR, aVL, aVF) and unipolar leads
q: what are the augmented leads
what does unipolar mean on an ECG
how are augmented leads different from leads I, II and III
cards.x:
The augmented leads are augmented vector right (aVR), augmented vector left (aVL) and augmented vector foot (aVF). They are unipolar, meaning each one uses only a single real electrode. The machine builds the other pole itself, a theoretical negative reference point. It also amplifies the signal, which is where the word augmented comes from.

Quick contrast with leads I, II and III. Those are bipolar, with a real positive and a real negative electrode. The augmented leads use one physical lead and a made-up negative.

The six limb leads together, I, II, III and the three augmented leads, form the first six leads of the 12-lead tracing. They are used to determine the axis.

cards.t: Chest (precordial) lead placement, V1 to V6
k: V1 V2 V3 V4 V5 V6
q: where do the chest leads go
where is V4 placed
what view of the heart do the chest leads give
cards.x:
The six chest, or precordial, leads are unipolar. They use the central terminal (the machine's made-up negative reference) as their negative pole. They need very specific placement, and they give a horizontal view of the heart.

- First chest lead (V1): fourth intercostal space (the gap between ribs), just right of the sternum.
- Second chest lead (V2): fourth intercostal space, just left of the sternum.
- Third chest lead (V3): directly between the second and fourth chest leads.
- Fourth chest lead (V4): fifth intercostal space at the midclavicular line.
- Fifth (V5) and sixth (V6) chest leads: level with the fourth, at the left anterior axillary line and the midaxillary line.

Memory trick: the first two chest leads sit in the same space on either side of the breastbone. The fourth drops one space down. The fourth, fifth and sixth then run along one level line out to the side.

cards.t: Contiguous leads and which wall of the heart each looks at
q: what are contiguous leads
which leads look at the inferior wall
which leads look at the lateral wall
cards.x:
Contiguous leads are two or more leads that look at the same area of the heart. Reading them together is how you tell which part of the heart a change is coming from. The groups are:

- V1 (first chest lead) and V2 (second chest lead): septal wall.
- V3 (third chest lead) and V4 (fourth chest lead): anterior wall of the left ventricle.
- I, augmented vector left (aVL), V5 (fifth chest lead) and V6 (sixth chest lead): lateral wall of the left ventricle.
- II, III and augmented vector foot (aVF): inferior wall.

Put another way, the contiguous groups are V1 to V4 (anterior and septal), I, aVL, V5 and V6 (lateral), and II, III and aVF (inferior). Augmented vector right (aVR) has clinical significance, but it is not usually used in basic 12-lead interpretation.

cards.t: Reading ECG paper: boxes, time and voltage
q: how long is a small box on an ECG
what is the paper speed of an ECG
what is standard calibration
cards.x:
An electrocardiogram (ECG) is printed on grid paper moving at 25 millimeters per second. Left to right is time; up and down is voltage.

- Small box: 1 millimeter tall and 0.04 seconds wide.
- Large box: five small boxes, so 5 millimeters tall and 0.2 seconds wide.

So five large boxes make one second, and 30 large boxes make the six-second strip used for counting the rate. Standard calibration is one large box (0.2 seconds) wide and two large boxes (10 millimeters) tall.

Be careful with units: a small box is 0.04 seconds (40 milliseconds), not 0.04 milliseconds.

cards.t: The P wave and the PR interval
q: what does the P wave represent
what is a normal PR interval
what happens during the PR interval
cards.x:
The P wave is atrial depolarization: the atria firing, whatever its shape. A normal one is round and upright in lead II, 2.5 millimeters or less tall and under 0.12 seconds wide.

The PR interval runs from the start of the P wave to the start of the QRS (the spike made by the ventricles). It covers the whole trip of the impulse: the atria firing, the hold-up in the atrioventricular node, and then the bundle of His, the bundle branches and the Purkinje network, all before the ventricles fire. That makes it the busiest time in the cardiac cycle.

Normal is 0.12 to 0.20 seconds (3 to 5 small boxes), and it should be constant across the strip.

cards.t: The QRS complex and its Q, R and S waves
q: what is the QRS complex
what is a normal QRS duration
what is the difference between the Q, R and S waves
cards.x:
The QRS (the tall spike on the tracing) is ventricular depolarization: the ventricles firing. It is called a complex because it combines three waves, though not every rhythm shows all three.

- Q wave: the first negative (downward) deflection after the PR interval. It is septal depolarization, moving away from lead II. It is under 0.04 seconds, low and not always visible.
- R wave: the first positive (upward) deflection, as depolarization moves toward lead II.
- S wave: the first negative deflection after the R wave. It must dip below the baseline to count as a true S wave.

The rule of thumb is direction: movement toward lead II draws an upright wave, movement away draws a downward one. A normal QRS is under 0.12 seconds, narrow with sharp points. A QRS of 0.12 seconds or more means conduction through the ventricles is abnormal.

cards.t: The J point, ST segment, T wave and the true baseline
q: what is the ST segment
where do I judge the baseline on an ECG
what is the T wave
cards.x:
Right after the QRS (the spike made by the ventricles) comes a flat stretch. The point where the QRS ends and that flat stretch begins is the J point. It should sit at the baseline, though 1 millimeter of variance is allowed.

The ST segment is the flat stretch between ventricular firing and recovery. It is where the ventricles hold their contraction to empty. It should also sit at baseline. The T wave that follows is ventricular repolarization, the recovery. It is asymmetric: a slow upstroke and a sharp downstroke.

The true baseline, the isoelectric line, is judged in the TP (T-to-P) segment, from the end of the T wave to the next P wave. That is the heart's resting state. Do not judge it in the PR segment, because the impulse is still crossing the atrioventricular node then.

One naming rule: an interval contains at least one wave, while a segment is just the flat line between waves.

cards.t: The QT interval and the corrected QT (QTc)
q: what does the QT interval measure
what is a normal QT interval
what is the QTc and when is it high risk
cards.x:
The QT interval measures all the ventricular electrical activity in one cycle, from the start of the QRS (the main spike) to the end of the T wave. Normal is 350 to 450 milliseconds in males and 360 to 460 in females.

The QTc is the QT (the interval above) corrected for heart rate. It has the same normal values as the QT. Above 450 milliseconds (460 in women) up to 500 it counts as borderline, and above 500 milliseconds it is high risk.

cards.t: Four ways to calculate heart rate from a strip
q: how do you calculate heart rate on an ECG
when do you use the six-second method
which heart rate method is most accurate
cards.x:
There are four ways to turn a strip into a rate, and each has a best use.

- Six-second method: count the ventricular spikes (QRS complexes) in a six-second strip, or 30 large boxes, and multiply by 10. Count P waves times 10 for the atrial rate. It is the most commonly used and works on irregular rhythms because it counts every beat. Fourteen complexes gives 140 per minute.
- Count-down method: start at an R wave on a heavy line, then count down 300, 150, 100, 75, 60, 50 for the following heavy lines. It is unreliable below 50 and on irregular rhythms.
- 300 method: 300 divided by the large boxes between consecutive R waves. For regular rhythms only. Four boxes gives 75; six boxes gives 50, which is below 60 and so a bradycardia.
- 1500 method: 1500 divided by the small boxes between consecutive R waves. This is the most accurate.

cards.t: Is the rhythm regular or irregular?
q: how do you tell if a rhythm is regular
what are R to R intervals
how do you use calipers on an ECG
cards.x:
Regularity is about spacing. Compare the distance between each pair of consecutive R waves, called the R to R interval. If the same distance separates every pair, the rhythm is regular. If the R to R intervals change from beat to beat, it is irregular.

Most irregular rhythms are obvious at a glance. When you are not sure, use calipers (a measuring tool), or just mark the distance on the edge of a sheet of paper. Walk it along the strip to see whether each beat lands on schedule. The same idea works with P to P intervals when you want to know whether the atrial beats are regular.

cards.t: The five-step systematic approach to a rhythm strip
k: rate regularity P waves PR QRS
how to read a rhythm strip
q: what are the five steps of rhythm interpretation
what order do I analyze an ECG strip in
what questions do I ask about the P waves
cards.x:
Use the same five steps, in the same order, on every strip so you never skip one:

- Step 1, rate: under 60, 60 to 100, or over 100.
- Step 2, regularity: are the consecutive R to R intervals equal?
- Step 3, P waves: look at them closely.
- Step 4, PR interval: 0.12 to 0.20 seconds, and constant?
- Step 5, QRS (the main spike): narrow, under 0.12 seconds, or wide?

The P wave step has several questions. Are they all the same shape? Is there one before each QRS? Are they married to the QRS, meaning each P wave is causing its QRS? Are they normal: round, upright in lead II, 2.5 millimeters or less, under 0.12 seconds? Is the PR interval constant? Atrioventricular nodal blocks, accessory pathways and alternate pacemaker sites can push the PR interval outside its normal range.

cards.t: What P waves tell you about where a rhythm starts
q: what does a P wave before every QRS mean
how do I know a rhythm comes from the sinoatrial node
what does it mean if there are no P waves
cards.x:
P waves are your clue to where the impulse started. A P wave married to every QRS (the spike made by the ventricles) means the rhythm is atrial in origin, and that is true whatever the QRS looks like. If the P waves are also uniform and upright, they point to the sinoatrial node. The classic picture is one uniform upright P wave before each narrow QRS at a constant PR interval. The P waves are married to the QRS complexes.

If you see QRS complexes with no P waves, the atria are not producing normal P waves. The impulse may have started below the atria, as in a junctional or ventricular rhythm, or the atria may be firing chaotically, as in atrial fibrillation.

cards.t: Normal sinus rhythm
q: what are the criteria for normal sinus rhythm
what does normal sinus rhythm look like
what rate is normal sinus rhythm
cards.x:
Normal sinus rhythm is the baseline everything else is compared against. It is the heart following its natural chain of command, with the sinoatrial node setting the pace. Run through the five steps and every one comes out normal:

- Rate: 60 to 100 per minute.
- Regularity: regular.
- P waves: normal, present, and married to the QRS (the spike made by the ventricles).
- PR interval: normal, 0.12 to 0.20 seconds, and constant.
- QRS: narrow.

If any one of these is off, the rhythm gets a different name.

cards.t: Sinus bradycardia and sinus tachycardia
q: what is sinus bradycardia
what is sinus tachycardia
what makes a rhythm sinus
cards.x:
Both are normal sinus rhythm with only the rate changed. Sinus bradycardia is a rate under 60 per minute. Sinus tachycardia is a rate over 100. Both are regular, with a normal PR interval of 0.12 to 0.20 seconds.

What makes them sinus is the P waves: present, normal and married to the QRS (the spike made by the ventricles). If those are right, the impulse comes from the sinoatrial node and the name depends only on the rate. The QRS is usually narrow, but it can be wide when conduction through the ventricles is abnormal, and that does not change the name.

Two examples: R waves about six large boxes apart works out to about 50 per minute (bradycardia), and R waves two large boxes apart means 150 (tachycardia).

cards.t: Sinus arrhythmia (respiratory sinus arrhythmia)
q: what is sinus arrhythmia
is sinus arrhythmia dangerous
how do you recognize sinus arrhythmia
cards.x:
Sinus arrhythmia is a harmless variation in the spacing between heartbeats, most commonly seen in children. It follows the person's breathing: the rate rises as they breathe in and falls as they breathe out. You can literally watch the tracing track the patient's breaths.

Every beat is a normal sinus beat with a P wave, a normal PR interval and a narrow ventricular spike (QRS complex), so all the complexes look normal. The only thing that changes is the timing, which makes the rhythm irregular. The measuring rule is that the longest R to R interval exceeds the shortest by more than 0.16 seconds. Note that no beats are missing, which separates it from a sinus block.

cards.t: Sinus exit block (sinus block)
q: what is sinus exit block
why is the gap a multiple of the P to P interval
how is sinus block different from sinus arrhythmia
cards.x:
In sinus exit block the sinus node keeps firing normally, but some of its impulses are blocked and never get out. The result is that one or more whole cardiac cycles are absent: no P wave, no ventricular spike (QRS complex) and no T wave.

Because the node never actually stopped, its timing is preserved. The missing beat would have landed exactly on schedule, so the gap is an exact multiple of the normal cycle, and the beats march out when activity resumes. For example, a 2.2-second gap on a strip with 1.1-second cycles is exactly two cycles.

That is the clue that separates it from a sinus pause or arrest, where the rhythm restarts on a new timing.

cards.t: Sick sinus syndrome
k: sinus exit block pause and arrest together
q: what is sick sinus syndrome
which rhythms make up sick sinus syndrome
is sick sinus syndrome common
cards.x:
Sick sinus syndrome is not a single rhythm. It is when a patient has sinus node problems such as sinus exit block, sinus pause and sinus arrest, often more than one on the same strip. It is mostly a disease of older adults. Think of it as a sinoatrial node that misbehaves in several different ways instead of in one consistent way.

So if you see a gap in the rhythm, identify which type it is. If one patient shows exit block, pause and arrest, the overall diagnosis is sick sinus syndrome.

cards.t: Sinus pause versus sinus arrest
q: what is the difference between sinus pause and sinus arrest
does the P to P interval march out after a pause
how many missed cycles define sinus arrest
cards.x:
In a sinus pause, the sinus node stops firing and then starts again. Because it restarts, the next beat does not land on the old schedule, so the gap is not a multiple of the P to P interval. After the flat gap the rhythm resumes on a new timing.

Sinus arrest is the same thing but longer: at least three cycles are missed. It also resets the node, so the beats afterward do not march out either.

So pause and arrest differ only in the length of the gap, and both differ from exit block, whose gap is an exact multiple of the cycle. Where P waves are present, they are normal and married to the ventricular spike (QRS complex), and the PR interval is normal.

cards.t: The sinus rhythms compared side by side
q: how do sinus bradycardia, tachycardia and arrhythmia differ
which sinus rhythms are irregular
how do I tell the sinus rhythms apart
cards.x:
Start with the rate and whether the rhythm is regular, then look at what is wrong.

- Normal sinus rhythm, sinus bradycardia and sinus tachycardia: all regular and all normal apart from the rate, which is 60 to 100, under 60 and over 100 per minute.
- Sinus arrhythmia: 60 to 100 per minute, but the R to R spacing varies with breathing. No beats are missing.
- Sinus exit block: whole cycles are missing, but the P to P intervals still march out on schedule.
- Sinus pause and sinus arrest: the node stops and restarts, so P to P does not march out. Arrest is a pause with at least three cycles missed.
- Sick sinus syndrome: sinus node problems such as exit block, pause and arrest, often more than one in one patient.

The first three are regular and differ only in rate. In the other rhythms the spacing is off, either because it varies or because beats are missing.

cards.t: Why sinus arrhythmia follows breathing
q: why does heart rate rise when you breathe in
what causes respiratory sinus arrhythmia
is sinus arrhythmia a dysfunction
cards.x:
Sinus arrhythmia is normal physiology, not sinus node dysfunction. Breathing itself changes the rate through a chain of events.

On inspiration, pressure inside the chest (intrathoracic pressure) falls, and arterial pressure falls with it. The baroreceptors, the pressure sensors, respond, vagal tone (the vagus nerve's braking effect on the heart) is suppressed, and the heart rate rises.

On exhalation the opposite happens, and the rate falls. So the sinoatrial node is working normally. It is just being nudged up and down with every breath.

cards.t: Conduction problem versus firing problem in sinus node dysfunction
q: why does exit block march out but pause does not
is sinus exit block a firing or a conduction problem
what happens when the sinoatrial node fails
cards.x:
The sinoatrial node normally fires at 60 to 100 per minute and keeps the lower pacemakers quiet. When it fails, the atrioventricular node (40 to 60) and then the Purkinje network (20 to 40) take over.

The three sinus node problems split into two kinds:

- Exit block is a conduction problem. The node fires on time, but the impulse is blocked from leaving it. The timing is preserved, so the beats march out.
- Pause and arrest are firing problems. The node stops and starts again, which resets the cycle, so the beats do not march out. Arrest means at least three missed cycles.

Picture a metronome. In exit block it keeps ticking and you just do not hear some ticks. In a pause it stops and is restarted, so the ticking begins on a new beat. Sick sinus syndrome is the umbrella for sinus node problems like these, often more than one in the same patient.

cards.t: Premature atrial complex
q: what is a premature atrial complex
how do I recognize a premature atrial complex on a strip
what causes premature atrial complexes
cards.x:
A premature atrial complex is an early extra beat that starts somewhere in the atria other than the sinoatrial node. That out-of-place spot is called an ectopic site, and it can be one spot or several. It usually happens because the ectopic cells have increased automaticity. That means they have become overactive and fire before the sinoatrial node is due.

On the strip, the beat arrives early and carries its own P wave, whose shape differs from the sinus P waves. It is usually followed by a narrow QRS (the spike made by the ventricles). Everything else in the rhythm is normal, so the early beat is the only odd one out.

cards.t: Premature junctional complex
q: what is a premature junctional complex
where is the P wave on a premature junctional beat
are premature junctional complexes dangerous
cards.x:
A premature junctional complex is an early beat that comes from the atrioventricular junction, the area around the atrioventricular node. Like the premature atrial complex, it comes from increased automaticity, an overactive spot that fires before the next beat is expected. It arrives before the next expected R wave.

The giveaway is the P wave, which behaves the way it does for any junctional beat: there is none, it is upside down (inverted), or it comes after the QRS (the spike made by the ventricles) instead of before it. The beat itself is early and narrow.

The reassuring part: isolated premature junctional complexes have no clinical significance.

cards.t: Premature ventricular complex
q: what is a premature ventricular complex
how do I recognize a premature ventricular complex
why do premature ventricular complexes matter
cards.x:
A premature ventricular complex is an early beat that starts in the ventricles. It arrives before the next expected R wave, and it looks different from a normal beat because it does not travel the normal conduction route:

- Wide and abnormal-looking: the QRS (the spike made by the ventricles) is typically over 0.12 seconds.
- No P wave in front of it.
- The T wave points the opposite way from the QRS, which is called contralateral.

The concern is frequent ones, especially in groups, because they can reduce cardiac output, the amount of blood the heart pumps.

cards.t: R on T phenomenon
q: what is R on T
why is R on T dangerous
what can a premature ventricular complex on the T wave cause
cards.x:
R on T is a premature ventricular complex whose R wave lands on the T wave of the beat before it. The T wave is the ventricles recovering. The relative refractory period falls there. That is a window when the muscle is still fragile and can be set off by a stimulus.

That is why the timing matters. A premature ventricular complex that falls in that window can set off ventricular tachycardia or ventricular fibrillation. So the timing of the early beat, not just its presence, is what makes R on T important.

cards.t: Couplets, triplets, multifocal beats and runs of ventricular complexes
q: what is a couplet
what is the difference between unifocal and multifocal premature ventricular complexes
when do premature ventricular complexes become ventricular tachycardia
cards.x:
Premature ventricular complexes can be grouped and described by how they line up and how they look:

- Two in a row is a couplet; three in a row is a triplet.
- If they all have the same shape, they come from one focus (unifocal). If the shapes differ, there are several foci (multifocal).
- Three in a row has two names depending on speed: a triplet, or ventricular tachycardia when three or more come in a row at a fast rate. A brief run is nonsustained and needs evaluation.

The shape is a clue to the source: identical copies mean one irritable spot, and different shapes mean several.

cards.t: Bigeminy, trigeminy and quadrigeminy
q: what is bigeminy
what is the difference between bigeminy and trigeminy
can premature atrial complexes occur in a pattern
cards.x:
These words describe a repeating pattern of premature beats, and they work for premature atrial, junctional and ventricular complexes alike. The prefix tells you how often the early beat appears:

- Bigeminy: every other beat is premature (one normal beat, one early beat, repeating).
- Trigeminy: every third beat is premature (two normal beats, then an early one).
- Quadrigeminy: every fourth beat is premature (three normal beats, then an early one).

A useful memory hook: bi means two, tri means three and quadri means four. Count the beats in one repeating group and it gives you the name.

cards.t: Telling premature atrial, junctional and ventricular beats apart
k: premature atrial vs junctional vs ventricular
q: how do I tell premature atrial from junctional from ventricular beats
what is different about the T wave in a ventricular premature beat
what do I look at first on an early beat
cards.x:
All three premature beats come early, before the next expected R wave. What differs is where they start, which shows in the P wave and the QRS (the spike made by the ventricles).

- Atrial: starts in the atria outside the sinoatrial node. P wave present but a different shape. Usually narrow QRS. Normal T wave.
- Junctional: starts in the atrioventricular junction. P wave none, inverted or after the QRS. Usually narrow QRS. Normal T wave.
- Ventricular: starts in the ventricles. No P wave. Wide, abnormal QRS, typically over 0.12 seconds, and the T wave goes opposite the QRS.

The best shortcut is narrow or wide first. A narrow early beat came from above the ventricles, so check its P wave to choose atrial or junctional. A wide early beat with an opposite T wave and no P wave is ventricular.

cards.t: Escape beats and escape rhythms
q: what is an escape beat
what is the difference between a premature beat and an escape beat
which pacemaker takes over when the one above fails
cards.x:
An escape beat is the heart's backup plan. It comes late, past the point where the next R wave was expected, because the pacemaker above has failed or slowed. A lower pacemaker steps in and fires instead. That is the opposite of a premature beat, which comes early.

- Junctional escape beat: the sinoatrial node fails to fire or fires too slowly, so a late narrow beat appears after a pause. The sinus node then resets.
- Junctional escape rhythm: the escape beats become the rhythm. The atrioventricular node is now the main pacemaker, suppresses the sinoatrial node, and fires at 40 to 60 per minute, regular.
- Ventricular escape complex: both the sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodes fail, so a late wide beat appears.
- Idioventricular rhythm: the Purkinje network takes over as the primary pacemaker, regular at 20 to 40 per minute, wide, with no P waves.

cards.t: Where the P wave goes in a junctional rhythm
q: why is the P wave inverted in a junctional rhythm
why can the P wave be missing or after the QRS
what is the PR interval in a junctional rhythm
cards.x:
A junctional impulse starts in the middle and spreads both ways at once: up into the atria and down the bundle of His toward the ventricles. The position of the P wave depends on which arrives first.

- Atria first: the atria fire from the bottom up, so the wave points away from positive lead II. This gives an inverted P wave just before the QRS (the spike made by the ventricles), with a short PR interval, under 0.12 seconds.
- Both at the same time, or the atria are never fired: no visible P wave, because the QRS hides it.
- Ventricles first: the P wave appears after the QRS.

So in a junctional rhythm the P wave is absent or inverted, and if it is there at all it sits right before or after the QRS.

cards.t: Junctional escape, accelerated junctional rhythm and junctional tachycardia
q: what is the difference between junctional escape rhythm and junctional tachycardia
what is accelerated junctional rhythm
what are the P waves and QRS like in a junctional rhythm
cards.x:
These three are the same junctional picture at three different speeds. The rate is the only thing that changes the name:

- Junctional escape rhythm: 40 to 60 per minute.
- Accelerated junctional rhythm: 60 to 100 per minute.
- Junctional tachycardia: over 100 per minute.

The picture is shared. P waves are absent, or inverted just before or after the QRS (the spike made by the ventricles). If a PR interval can be measured, it is under 0.12 seconds. The QRS is narrow or wide, most commonly narrow.

cards.t: Idioventricular rhythm and accelerated idioventricular rhythm
q: what is idioventricular rhythm
what rate is idioventricular rhythm
what is accelerated idioventricular rhythm
cards.x:
Idioventricular rhythm is what you see when the ventricles pace themselves. The Purkinje network is the one doing the pacing, and it is the slowest backup pacemaker.

- Rate: 20 to 40 per minute. In the accelerated form it runs 40 to 100.
- Regular.
- P waves and PR interval: none.
- QRS (the spike made by the ventricles): wide, longer than 0.12 seconds.

The wide QRS follows from where it starts. A junctional impulse still travels the normal pathway into the ventricles, so its QRS is most commonly narrow. An idioventricular impulse starts below that pathway, so the complex comes out wide.

cards.t: Junctional rhythm versus idioventricular rhythm
q: how do I tell a junctional rhythm from an idioventricular rhythm
why is a junctional QRS narrow but an idioventricular QRS wide
what are the intrinsic rates of the junction and the Purkinje network
cards.x:
Both are regular backup rhythms, so the question is how to tell them apart.

- Pacemaker: junctional comes from the atrioventricular node (compact zone); idioventricular comes from the Purkinje network.
- Intrinsic rate: junctional 40 to 60 (accelerated 60 to 100, tachycardia over 100); idioventricular 20 to 40 (accelerated 40 to 100).
- P waves: junctional absent or inverted before or after the QRS (the spike made by the ventricles); idioventricular none.
- QRS: junctional is most commonly narrow; idioventricular is wide, over 0.12 seconds.

The QRS is the quickest clue. A junctional impulse still travels the normal pathway into the ventricles, so it is most commonly narrow. An idioventricular beat does not, so it comes out wide.

cards.t: Wandering atrial pacemaker and multifocal atrial tachycardia
q: what is multifocal atrial tachycardia
how is wandering atrial pacemaker different from multifocal atrial tachycardia
why does the P wave shape change
cards.x:
In these rhythms, at least three different spots in the atria compete to act as the pacemaker. Each one fires with its own P wave shape. So the P waves keep changing, and so do the PR interval, the P to P intervals and the R to R intervals. The rhythm is irregular.

The two are the same pattern at different speeds:

- Wandering atrial pacemaker: rate under 100.
- Multifocal atrial tachycardia: rate over 100.

The key finding for both is at least three different P wave shapes, still married to the QRS (the spike made by the ventricles). The QRS can be narrow or wide.

cards.t: Atrial flutter
q: what is atrial flutter
what does atrial flutter look like on a strip
why is atrial flutter called sawtooth
cards.x:
Atrial flutter is a very fast, organized atrial rhythm caused by a reentry circuit, an electrical loop that keeps circling. The loop is most often in the right atrium and is set up by chamber enlargement or by scarred or ischemic (poorly supplied with blood) tissue.

The atria fire at about 300 times per minute. On paper this draws a sawtooth pattern, which is pathognomonic, meaning that sight alone points to flutter. The sawtooth waves are called flutter waves (F waves), and they replace the P waves. There is no PR interval, and the QRS (the spike made by the ventricles) is narrow or wide.

The ventricular rate is lower than the atrial rate because only some flutter waves get through to the ventricles.

cards.t: Counting the atrial flutter ratio (2:1, 3:1, variable conduction)
q: how do I count the ratio in atrial flutter
what does 2:1 flutter mean
what is atrial flutter with variable conduction
cards.x:
The ventricular rate in atrial flutter depends on how many flutter waves pass for each QRS (the spike made by the ventricles). That count is the ratio, and you document it. Two flutter waves per QRS is atrial flutter with a 2:1 ratio, three is 3:1, and so on.

To count, draw a line through the peaks of the flutter waves, then count the troughs between one QRS and the next. A notch at the end of the QRS counts as a flutter wave too.

If the ratio stays the same, the rhythm is regular. If the ratio changes, the rhythm is irregular, and it is documented as atrial flutter with variable conduction. In that case the flutter waves stay constant (about 300) while the R to R intervals change.

cards.t: Atrial fibrillation
q: what is atrial fibrillation
what does irregularly irregular mean
what are the types of atrial fibrillation
cards.x:
Atrial fibrillation is the most treated cardiac arrhythmia. Many places in the atria fire in a disorganized way and suppress the sinoatrial node. Instead of contracting, the atria quiver, so the atrial kick is lost. The atrial kick is the 20 to 30 percent of ventricular filling that depends on the atria actually squeezing; the other 70 to 80 percent is passive.

On the strip there are no P waves, only fibrillatory (f) waves, a wobbly baseline. The atrial rate cannot be determined and the ventricular rate varies. The rhythm is irregularly irregular, with no repeating pattern at all. There is no PR interval, and the QRS (the spike made by the ventricles) is narrow or wide.

There are three types:

- Paroxysmal: converts back without intervention.
- Persistent: lasts more than 7 days, or needs a drug or electrical cardioversion to stop.
- Permanent: ongoing, and no further attempt is made to restore normal rhythm.

cards.t: Atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia (supraventricular tachycardia)
q: what is atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia
what causes supraventricular tachycardia
what are pseudo S waves
cards.x:
Atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia, the most common kind of paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia (and often simply called supraventricular tachycardia), is a regular, narrow-complex tachycardia caused by a reentry circuit. Picture a loop: an impulse goes down one pathway and returns up the other, circling over and over. The loop uses the slow and the fast pathways, and it is usually set off by an ectopic beat, typically a premature atrial complex.

On the strip: rate 150 to 300, regular, P waves not visible (or retrograde, running backward), no PR interval (or an RP (R-to-P) interval), and a narrow QRS (the spike made by the ventricles).

- Typical (most common): the circuit goes counterclockwise down the slow tract and up the fast tract. There are no P waves, or backward P waves buried at the end of the QRS, called pseudo S waves.
- Atypical (rare): down the fast tract and up the slow. The retrograde P waves are clearly visible, with an RP interval instead of a PR.

cards.t: Flutter, fibrillation, nodal reentry and multifocal tachycardia compared
k: atrial flutter vs atrial fibrillation vs supraventricular tachycardia
q: how do I tell atrial flutter from atrial fibrillation
which supraventricular rhythm is regular
which supraventricular rhythms have a narrow QRS
cards.x:
Four supraventricular rhythms can look alike, so compare what the atria are doing and how regular the ventricles are:

- Atrial flutter: sawtooth flutter waves at about 300. The ventricular rate is set by the ratio. Regular, or irregular with variable conduction. No PR interval.
- Atrial fibrillation: wobbly fibrillatory waves, rate indeterminate. Ventricular rate variable. Irregularly irregular. No PR interval.
- Nodal reentry (supraventricular tachycardia): atrial activity not visible, or retrograde. Rate 150 to 300. Regular.
- Multifocal atrial tachycardia: P waves of three or more shapes. Rate over 100. Irregular. PR interval variable.

The QRS (the spike made by the ventricles) can be narrow or wide in flutter, fibrillation and multifocal tachycardia, but in nodal reentry it is usually narrow.

cards.t: Sinus tachycardia versus supraventricular tachycardia
k: rate does not name the rhythm
P or T wave between complexes
q: is a rate of 190 supraventricular tachycardia
how do I tell sinus tachycardia from supraventricular tachycardia
what if a wave could be a P wave or a T wave
cards.x:
The rate alone never names the rhythm. A fast rhythm with a sinus P wave in front of every QRS (the spike made by the ventricles) is sinus tachycardia, even at 190. It is not nodal reentry (the rhythm usually called supraventricular tachycardia).

The nodal reentry rhythm is the most common paroxysmal (starting and stopping suddenly) supraventricular tachycardia, often simply called supraventricular tachycardia. It is the regular narrow one with no visible P waves. So the P wave is what decides.

If you cannot tell whether a single wave sitting between two rapid complexes is a P wave or a T wave, call it a T wave.

cards.t: Why each supraventricular rhythm happens
q: what causes premature atrial complexes
what causes atrial flutter versus atrial fibrillation
why does atrial fibrillation matter for ventricular filling
cards.x:
Each of these rhythms comes from a different kind of electrical problem:

- Premature atrial complexes: increased automaticity of an ectopic atrial site, an overactive spot that fires early.
- Wandering pacemaker and multifocal atrial tachycardia: at least three atrial sites competing to be the pacemaker, so the P wave shape keeps changing.
- Atrial flutter: one reentry circuit, most often in the right atrium, in enlarged, scarred or ischemic tissue. The atrioventricular node lets only some flutter waves through, which gives the ratio.
- Atrial fibrillation: many atrial sites firing chaotically and suppressing the sinoatrial node. The atrial kick is lost, which is the 20 to 30 percent of ventricular filling that is not passive.
- Atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia: a reentry loop over a slow and a fast tract, usually started by a premature atrial complex. In the typical form it goes down the slow tract and up the fast.

cards.t: The three zones of the atrioventricular node
q: what are the three zones of the atrioventricular node
what does the compact zone do
which zone causes premature junctional complexes
cards.x:
The atrioventricular node is not one uniform block. It has three zones, each with its own job:

- Transition zone: receives the sinus impulse. It is very arrhythmogenic, meaning prone to starting abnormal beats, and it is where most premature junctional complexes come from.
- Compact zone: the core of the node. It slows conduction on purpose, which gives time for the atria to contract and the ventricles to fill. It resembles the sinus node and can act as the backup pacemaker.
- Trigger zone: sends the signal on down the bundle of His.

That built-in slowing in the compact zone is also why the PR interval has a pause in the middle of it.

cards.t: Ventricular tachycardia
q: what is ventricular tachycardia
what does ventricular tachycardia look like on a strip
can a patient with ventricular tachycardia have a pulse
cards.x:
Ventricular tachycardia is any fast rhythm that starts in the ventricles. It can occur with or without a pulse, and the strip cannot tell you which, so the patient has to be checked. It can be regular and monomorphic, meaning every complex has the same shape, or irregular and polymorphic.

On the strip:

- Rate: 100 to 300 per minute.
- Regular.
- QRS (the spike made by the ventricles): wide.
- No P waves. If any are present, they are dissociated, meaning not married to the QRS and not related to it.
- Typically no PR interval.

The irregular form, where the complexes change shape, is polymorphic ventricular tachycardia.

cards.t: Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (torsades de pointes)
q: what is torsades de pointes
why is it called twisting of the points
what causes torsades de pointes
cards.x:
Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia is an irregular ventricular tachycardia at 100 to 300 per minute, and the form that comes with a prolonged QT interval is called torsades de pointes. The name is French for twisting of the points, and it describes the look: the wide complexes swing from positive to negative around the baseline, changing shape and amplitude as they swell and shrink.

It is usually a consequence of a prolonged QT interval. So when a strip shows torsades, the useful step is to go back to an earlier tracing and look at the QT.

Quick contrast with ordinary ventricular tachycardia: that form is regular with identical complexes, while torsades is irregular with changing shapes.

cards.t: Ventricular fibrillation
q: what is ventricular fibrillation
why does ventricular fibrillation cause no pulse
what is the difference between fine ventricular fibrillation and asystole
cards.x:
Ventricular fibrillation is chaotic, uncoordinated firing from multiple spots in the ventricles. The muscle can't contract in an organized way, so it just quivers. With no ventricular contraction there is no cardiac output and no pulse.

On the strip there are no measurable P waves, T waves or ventricular spikes (QRS complexes). The rate is 300 to 500 per minute and irregular, with no PR interval.

Fine fibrillation has low-amplitude, small chaotic waves, while coarse has large chaotic waves. Fine fibrillation is not truly flat, but it can look almost flat, so asystole should be confirmed in a second lead. That is the difference from asystole, where the line really is flat.

cards.t: Asystole
q: what is asystole
how does ventricular fibrillation lead to asystole
how is asystole different from ventricular standstill
cards.x:
Asystole is a complete lack of electrical activity in the heart, with no pulse. On the monitor it is a flat line.

It is also where untreated ventricular fibrillation ends up: the chaotic fibrillatory waves give way, over time, to nothing.

Quick way to tell it from ventricular standstill: in asystole there are no P waves either, because there is no electrical activity at all. In ventricular standstill the atria are still firing, so regular upright P waves march across the strip.

cards.t: Pulseless electrical activity
q: what is pulseless electrical activity
why can pulseless electrical activity look like normal sinus rhythm
how do you diagnose pulseless electrical activity
cards.x:
Pulseless electrical activity means the monitor shows organized electrical activity, but there is no palpable pulse because the heart is not pumping effectively; classically it is described as no mechanical activity, though ultrasound can show weak contractions.

The strip alone cannot make the diagnosis. Pulseless electrical activity can look like any organized rhythm, even normal sinus rhythm. The classic picture is a normal-looking organized rhythm, even normal sinus, with no pulse. So the diagnosis comes from the patient (no pulse), not from the shape of the tracing.

cards.t: Ventricular standstill
q: what is ventricular standstill
how is ventricular standstill different from asystole
what is paroxysmal ventricular standstill
cards.x:
In ventricular standstill, the atria still contract but the ventricles do not. On the strip, obvious upright P waves march out regularly across the page with no ventricular spikes (QRS complexes) after them. With no ventricular contraction there is no detectable pulse and no cardiac output.

The contrast with asystole is the P waves: asystole has none, while standstill has a steady row of them.

Some patients have episodes, called paroxysmal ventricular standstill, where conducted beats, with their ventricular spikes, alternate with stretches of standstill where the P waves carry on alone.

cards.t: Ventricular tachycardia, torsades and ventricular fibrillation compared
q: how do I tell ventricular tachycardia from ventricular fibrillation
what is the difference between monomorphic and polymorphic ventricular tachycardia
does ventricular fibrillation ever have a pulse
cards.x:
These three share a ventricular origin, so the useful thing is how they differ:

- Ventricular tachycardia: organized, regular, identical complexes at 100 to 300 per minute. Wide QRS (the spike made by the ventricles). The patient may or may not have a pulse.
- Torsades (polymorphic ventricular tachycardia): organized but irregular, with wide twisting complexes at 100 to 300. Linked to a prolonged QT interval. Pulse present or not, since it is still a ventricular tachycardia.
- Ventricular fibrillation: chaotic, no measurable complexes, 300 to 500. There is never a pulse, because the heart muscle is not contracting and there is no output.

Three separations to hold. Ventricular tachycardia has one repeating shape and is regular, while the polymorphic form changes shape and is irregular; rate and width cannot separate them. Tachycardia has organized complexes, while fibrillation is chaos with no QRS. Fine fibrillation is small continuous waves, while asystole is a flat line.

cards.t: Paced rhythms: atrial and ventricular pacemakers
q: what does an atrial paced rhythm look like
what does a ventricular paced rhythm look like
how do I know the ventricle is captured
cards.x:
A pacemaker puts a sharp vertical spike on the tracing each time it fires. What follows the spike tells you which chamber it is pacing.

- Atrial pacemaker: it takes over for the sinoatrial node and depends on a working conduction pathway below it. A pacer spike is followed by a normal P wave, QRS (the spike made by the ventricles) and T wave, so the QRS is narrow and normal.
- Ventricular pacemaker: it paces the ventricles below the level of the atria. The tracing shows a possible P wave, a pacer spike, a wide QRS and a contralateral T wave, one pointing the opposite direction to the QRS.

A spike married to every QRS, a wide QRS and a contralateral T wave show that the ventricle is captured, meaning the pacemaker is really driving it.

Patients with a dual-chamber pacemaker, which is common, can have both: a spike before the P wave and another before each wide QRS.

cards.t: Atrioventricular blocks: the four types
q: what is an atrioventricular block
what are the four atrioventricular blocks
what is the difference between Wenckebach and Mobitz II
cards.x:
Atrioventricular blocks are a delay in, or a complete failure of, the conduction of an atrial impulse across the atrioventricular junction to the ventricles. The atria fire normally, and the problem is the handoff. There are four:

- First-degree: the impulse is delayed but always gets through.
- Second-degree type I: also called Wenckebach or Mobitz I.
- Second-degree type II: also called Mobitz II.
- Third-degree: complete heart block, where no impulse gets through.

A good way to hold them: the first-degree block delays everything, the two second-degree types drop some beats, and the third-degree block drops them all.

cards.t: First-degree atrioventricular block
q: what is first-degree atrioventricular block
what is the hallmark of first-degree block
does first-degree block drop beats
cards.x:
First-degree atrioventricular block is a benign delay. Conduction through the atrioventricular node is slowed, so every impulse takes longer than usual to reach the ventricles. Think of a delivery that is always late but always arrives.

The hallmark is a sinus rhythm with a PR interval beyond 0.2 seconds that stays consistently long from cycle to cycle. All the P waves are conducted, so nothing is dropped.

The rest of the strip looks normal. The rate is slow or normal, the rhythm is regular, the P waves are normal and married to the QRS (the spike made by the ventricles), and the QRS is narrow or wide.

cards.t: Second-degree type I block (Wenckebach, Mobitz I)
q: what is Wenckebach
what pattern does second-degree type I block make
why does the PR interval get longer before a dropped beat
cards.x:
Second-degree type I block, called Wenckebach, comes from a problem in the atrioventricular node. Conduction through the node slows a little more with every beat, as if the node were tiring. Finally one impulse is not conducted at all. Then the cycle begins over.

The classic pattern is a PR interval that gets longer, longer, longer. Then a P wave comes with no QRS (the spike made by the ventricles) after it. That is a dropped beat. This makes grouped beats, with the pauses falling at the dropped beat.

On the strip:

- rate slow or normal
- irregular (from the dropped beat)
- P waves normal and married to the QRS, except for the dropped one
- PR increasing
- QRS narrow or wide

cards.t: Second-degree type II block (Mobitz II)
q: what is Mobitz II
what is the hallmark of second-degree type II block
why is Mobitz II more serious than Wenckebach
cards.x:
Second-degree type II is less common than type I but more serious. It is almost always a sign of underlying disease of the conduction system, and it is possible for more than one beat to drop in a row.

The hallmark is a constant PR interval with some P waves that are not conducted, so the QRS (the spike made by the ventricles) is dropped. It is identified when at least two consecutive atrial impulses are conducted with constant PR intervals before the dropped QRS.

On the strip: rate slow or normal, irregular, P waves normal and married to the QRS except for the dropped beats, and the PR is normal or long but always constant. The QRS is usually, though not always, wide, from an accompanying bundle branch block. The block sits below the atrioventricular node, in the His-Purkinje system.

cards.t: Third-degree atrioventricular block (complete heart block)
q: what is third-degree heart block
what is the hallmark of complete heart block
why do the P waves march through the QRS in complete heart block
cards.x:
In third-degree block the atria and ventricles are working completely independently. The block is total, so no P waves are conducted through the atrioventricular junction.

That means two pacemakers are running at once. The sinoatrial node drives the atria. A lower escape pacemaker drives the ventricles: either the atrioventricular junction or the Purkinje and bundle-branch fibers. The atrial rate is faster than the ventricular rate.

The hallmark is regular P-P intervals unrelated to regular R-R intervals. So the P waves appear to march through the QRS (the spike made by the ventricles) and T wave of each beat. There is no PR interval. The QRS is narrow or wide depending on where the escape comes from. For example, take an atrial rate of 75 with a ventricular rate of 27 and a wide QRS. The wide QRS points to an escape pacemaker in the Purkinje or bundle-branch fibers.

cards.t: The four atrioventricular blocks compared
k: first second third degree block table
q: how do the four atrioventricular blocks differ
which heart block has a constant PR interval
which block has no relationship between P waves and QRS
cards.x:
Compare them by the PR interval, the dropped beats and whether P is married to the QRS (the spike made by the ventricles):

- First-degree: PR longer than 0.2 seconds and fixed. No dropped beats. Married. Regular. Benign.
- Second-degree type I: PR increases until a beat drops, one drop at the end of each group. Married except the dropped beat. Irregular. More common than type II.
- Second-degree type II: PR constant, normal or long. Some dropped beats, possibly more than one in a row. Married except the dropped beats. Irregular. Less common but more serious. QRS usually wide.
- Third-degree: no PR consistency, no P waves conducted at all. Not married, P waves march through. Regular P-P and regular R-R. A total block.

QRS width in first- and second-degree type I is narrow or wide, and in third-degree it depends on the escape origin.

cards.t: How to tell second-degree type I from type II
k: which block has more P waves than QRS
q: how do I tell type I from type II second-degree block
what is the trick for Wenckebach versus Mobitz II
how do I identify which heart block it is
cards.x:
Use this trick for second-degree blocks. Find the dropped beat, the P wave with no QRS (the spike made by the ventricles) after it. Then compare the PR interval of the cycle before the dropped beat with the PR of the cycle after it.

- If the two PR intervals are different, it is always type I. In type I the PR is longest just before the drop and resets shorter after it.
- If the two PR intervals are equal, it is type II, except in 2:1 block, where the two beats cannot tell you the type.

A broader shortcut for any block: more P waves than QRS complexes suggests a block. Then a lengthening PR means type I, a constant PR means type II, and a randomly changing PR means third-degree. A long PR with every P wave conducted is first-degree.

cards.t: Where each block sits: nodal versus infranodal
q: which blocks are in the atrioventricular node
where is a Mobitz II block located
what drives the ventricles in complete heart block
cards.x:
The location of the problem explains the patterns.

- First-degree: in the atrioventricular node. Conduction is slowed, but every impulse still gets through.
- Second-degree type I: also in the atrioventricular node. Conduction slows beat by beat until one impulse fails, as if the node were progressively tiring until it does not release an impulse, and then resetting. The P waves march out on time, and it is the node that falls behind.
- Second-degree type II: infranodal, meaning low, below the node at the His bundle, generally in the His-Purkinje system. It reflects disease of the conduction system.
- Third-degree: a total blockage at the junction. The sinoatrial node keeps driving the atria, while the ventricles are driven by an escape pacemaker below the block. From the atrioventricular junction, the QRS (the spike made by the ventricles) is narrow; from the Purkinje and bundle-branch fibers, it is wide.

cards.t: Why P waves are dissociated in ventricular tachycardia
k: P waves not married to QRS
q: why do P waves not match the QRS in ventricular tachycardia
what does dissociated mean
does ventricular tachycardia travel back to the atria
cards.x:
Ventricular tachycardia comes from a focus in the ventricles. The impulse often does not travel back up into the atria, so the atria usually carry on doing their own thing. Any P waves they still produce are dissociated from the QRS (the spike made by the ventricles), meaning they have no relationship with it.

That is why P waves in ventricular tachycardia, when you can see them at all, are not married to the QRS.

cards.t: What the ventricular rhythms mean for the patient
q: which rhythms have no pulse
can the strip tell me whether the patient has a pulse
what does torsades suggest
cards.x:
The strip shows the electrical activity, but what matters most is whether the heart is actually pumping, so the pulse is the question for each of these.

- Ventricular tachycardia: may come with or without a pulse, and the strip cannot tell you which.
- Torsades de pointes: usually a consequence of a prolonged QT interval, so look at the QT on the earlier tracing.
- Pulseless electrical activity: organized electrical activity but no palpable pulse (classically described as no mechanical activity), despite a normal-looking rhythm.
- Ventricular fibrillation, asystole and ventricular standstill: no pulse. In fibrillation the ventricles quiver without contracting. In asystole there is no electrical activity. In standstill the atria contract but the ventricles do not, so there is no cardiac output.

cards.t: How serious each block is and what causes third-degree block
k: inferior myocardial infarction and heart block
q: which heart blocks are benign
what causes third-degree heart block
why is Mobitz II more serious
cards.x:
The blocks differ a lot in how worrying they are.

- First-degree block is benign.
- Second-degree type II is less common but more serious than type I. It is almost always a sign of underlying conduction system disease, and it can drop more than one beat in a row.
- Third-degree block is a total block. Its most common causes are age-related fibrosis (scarring) of the atrioventricular conduction system and acute myocardial infarction (heart attack), especially inferior.

cards.t: Electrical axis: normal, left, right and extreme deviation
q: what is the electrical axis of the heart
what are the degrees for normal axis and axis deviation
what is no man's land on the axis wheel
cards.x:
The axis is the direction of the heart's mean electrical vector, the average direction the electrical impulse travels. Normally it points a little to the left and down. Age, medical history and disease, chronic or acute, can all shift it.

Think of the axis as a dial measured in degrees:

- Normal axis: -30 to +90 degrees.
- Left axis deviation: beyond -30 degrees, toward -90.
- Right axis deviation: beyond +90 degrees, toward 180.
- Extreme axis deviation, called no man's land: between -90 and 180 degrees.

One extra pointer: a negative lead III with the axis between 0 and -30 degrees is still a normal variant as long as lead II stays positive. Once lead II is mostly negative as well, the left deviation is pathological.

cards.t: Finding the axis quickly with leads I and aVF
q: how do I determine the axis from leads I and aVF
what do leads I and aVF look like in left axis deviation
how do I decide if a QRS is mostly positive or negative
cards.x:
You only need two leads. Leads I and aVF sit at either end of the normal sector, so together they pin the axis down quickly.

For each lead, look at the QRS (the spike made by the ventricles) and decide whether it is mostly positive or mostly negative. That just means asking whether the R wave or the S wave is bigger. Then read the combination:

- Both mostly positive: normal axis.
- Lead I positive, aVF negative: the axis is to the left; check lead II, because if it is mostly negative this is left axis deviation, and if it is still positive it is a normal variant.
- Lead I negative, aVF positive: right axis deviation.
- Both mostly negative: extreme axis deviation, no man's land.

cards.t: Causes of left, right and extreme axis deviation
k: wide complex tachycardia with extreme axis
q: what causes left axis deviation
what causes right axis deviation
what does extreme axis deviation suggest
cards.x:
Axis deviation is a clue to what is going on in the heart or lungs. You do not need to memorize every item. Here are some of the causes.

- Left axis deviation: past inferior infarction (heart attack), left anterior fascicular block, ventricular pacing, emphysema and hyperkalemia (high potassium).
- Right axis deviation: normal in children. Otherwise seen in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, pulmonary embolism, previous anterolateral infarction, septal defects, dextrocardia (heart on the right), left posterior fascicular block, reversed arm leads and right ventricular hypertrophy.
- Extreme axis deviation: emphysema, hyperkalemia, lead transposition, ventricular pacing and ventricular arrhythmia.

Because ventricular arrhythmia is on that last list, a wide-complex tachycardia with extreme axis deviation raises suspicion of ventricular tachycardia.

cards.t: The systematic read of a 12-lead tracing
q: what are the steps for reading a 12-lead
what do I check first on a 12-lead
what does a normal 12-lead read like
cards.x:
A 12-lead gets its own order of steps, so you do not jump straight to the dramatic finding. Start with a general impression: does it look good or does it look ugly? Next check the calibration, which should be standard: one big box wide and two big boxes tall. Then find the axis (normal, left, right or extreme) and assess the QRS (the spike made by the ventricles): narrow or wide, any bundle branch blocks, any fascicular blocks? After that look for hypertrophy and chamber enlargement, and last come the ST segment and T wave changes: ischemia, injury and infarct.

A normal tracing reads: looks good, standard calibration, normal axis, QRS within normal limits, no hypertrophy or enlargement, no ischemia or infarct.

cards.t: The J point rule for telling right from left bundle branch block
q: how do I tell right from left bundle branch block
what is the J point rule
do I need to see bunny ears for right bundle branch block
cards.x:
Both bundle branch blocks need a QRS (the spike made by the ventricles) of 0.12 seconds or longer, which is three small boxes. After that, the side is decided in V1 (the chest lead just right of the sternum) with the J point rule: find the J point, where the QRS ends, and travel backwards from it to the very first deflection you meet.

- First deflection negative (an rS pattern): left bundle branch block.
- First deflection positive (an rSR pattern, with a terminal R wave): right bundle branch block.

You may have heard the bunny ears of right bundle branch block in V1. Don't rely on them, because the block takes many V1 shapes. The constant is the positive first deflection backward from the J point.

cards.t: Left bundle branch block
q: what does left bundle branch block look like
what are the criteria for left bundle branch block
why are there no Q waves in left bundle branch block
cards.x:
Left bundle branch block has four features to check:

- QRS (the spike made by the ventricles) of 0.12 seconds or longer.
- An rS pattern in V1 (the chest lead just right of the sternum): travel back from the J point and the very first deflection is negative.
- Notching of the QRS in the lateral leads, namely I, aVL, V5 (fifth chest lead) and V6 (sixth chest lead), the double QRS complex phenomenon, best seen in V6.
- No Q waves in the lateral leads.

The notch is a picture of the two ventricles firing one after the other: the right ventricle first, then the left.

cards.t: Right bundle branch block
q: what does right bundle branch block look like
what are the criteria for right bundle branch block
what is a slurred S wave
cards.x:
Right bundle branch block is the same kind of block on the right side. The QRS (the spike made by the ventricles) is 0.12 seconds or longer, and the findings are:

- V1 (the chest lead just right of the sternum) shows an rSR pattern. Travel back from the J point and the very first deflection is positive, a terminal R wave.
- The lateral leads, namely I, aVL, V5 (fifth chest lead) and V6 (sixth chest lead), show slurred S waves. This is the double QRS complex phenomenon, best seen in V6.

The familiar bunny ears are one way V1 can look. There are many shapes, including rR', rsR', rSR', rSr' and others. Every one of them ends with a positive deflection before the J point, and that is the feature to trust.

cards.t: Right versus left bundle branch block compared
q: how do right and left bundle branch block differ
which bundle branch block can mimic a heart attack
which ventricle is late in left bundle branch block
cards.x:
The two blocks share a QRS (the spike made by the ventricles) of 0.12 seconds or longer. The differences are in the details:

- V1 (the chest lead just right of the sternum): right bundle branch block is rSR, with a positive first deflection back from the J point. Left is rS, with a negative one.
- Lateral leads (I, aVL, V5 (fifth chest lead) and V6 (sixth chest lead)): right shows slurred S waves. Left shows a notched QRS with no Q waves.
- Ventricle depolarized late: right in right bundle branch block, left in left bundle branch block.
- Infarction mimic list: left bundle branch block (along with ventricular paced rhythms) is on it. Right bundle branch block is not.

So each block is named for the side whose ventricle fires late.

cards.t: Right atrial enlargement (P pulmonale)
q: what is P pulmonale
how do I recognize right atrial enlargement
what does the P wave look like in V1 in right atrial enlargement
cards.x:
P pulmonale is the electrocardiogram (ECG) sign of an enlarged right atrium. The P wave is the atria firing, so a bigger atrium changes its shape. In this case the wave becomes tall and peaked.

- In the limb leads (I, II and III): an upright P wave taller than 2.5 millimeters.
- In V1 (the chest lead just right of the sternum): a biphasic P wave, meaning it has an up part and a down part, with a larger positive first part and a smaller negative last part.

You do not need both. Evidence of P pulmonale in one of these leads is enough to confirm it; the criteria need not be met in every lead.

cards.t: Left atrial enlargement (P mitrale)
q: what is P mitrale
how do I recognize left atrial enlargement
what does the P wave look like in V1 in left atrial enlargement
cards.x:
P mitrale is the electrocardiogram (ECG) sign of an enlarged left atrium. Here the P wave becomes wide and humped:

- In the limb leads (I, II and III): an upright, humped P wave at least 0.12 seconds long, with the two humps at least 0.04 seconds apart.
- In V1 (the chest lead just right of the sternum): a biphasic P wave with a small positive first part and a large negative last part.

As with the right side, evidence in one lead is confirmatory, so the criteria need not be met in every lead.

cards.t: P pulmonale versus P mitrale: how to tell them apart
q: how do I tell right from left atrial enlargement
why is the P wave in V1 biphasic
which atrium makes the second half of the P wave
cards.x:
A quick memory line: pulmonale is tall, mitrale is wide.

- P pulmonale (right atrium): tall, peaked P wave in the limb leads, upright and over 2.5 millimeters. In V1 (the chest lead just right of the sternum), biphasic with a larger positive first part.
- P mitrale (left atrium): wide, humped P wave, at least 0.12 seconds with humps at least 0.04 apart. In V1, biphasic with a large negative last part.

Why does V1 split this way? The right atrium depolarizes first, which gives the positive start, and the left atrium depolarizes last, which gives the negative end. So the enlarged atrium owns the bigger half of the P wave. One lead meeting the criterion confirms either.

cards.t: Right ventricular hypertrophy and the strain pattern
k: R to S ratio V1 V2
q: what are the criteria for right ventricular hypertrophy
what is the strain pattern
what rules out right ventricular hypertrophy on an ECG
cards.x:
Right ventricular hypertrophy means the muscle wall of the right ventricle has thickened. The key criterion is an R to S ratio of 1 or more in V1 (the chest lead just right of the sternum) and V2 (the next lead to the left). In other words, more R wave than S wave.

Other findings support the diagnosis:

- Right atrial enlargement.
- Right axis deviation.
- A strain pattern: the ST segment runs from the J point into an inverted, asymmetrical T wave in V1 and V2.

This criterion is unreliable because some other things also give a tall R wave in V1: right bundle branch block, posterior wall infarction, and children under the age of 7 or 8.

cards.t: Left ventricular hypertrophy: the voltage criteria
k: R wave in aVL greater than 12
q: what are the criteria for left ventricular hypertrophy
how do I add up the voltage for left ventricular hypertrophy
what does left ventricular hypertrophy do to the axis
cards.x:
Left ventricular hypertrophy is a thickened left ventricle. The thick wall pulls the electrical vector to the left. So it can cause left axis deviation, along with deep S waves in V1 (the chest lead just right of the sternum) and V2 (the next lead to the left) and tall R waves in the lateral leads, namely I, aVL, V5 (fifth chest lead) and V6 (sixth chest lead).

It is present by any one of these three:

- The deeper S wave in V1 or V2 plus the taller R wave in V5 or V6 adds up to 35 millimeters or more.
- The R wave in aVL is greater than 12 millimeters.
- Any chest lead is greater than 45 millimeters.

For example, an S wave of 45 plus an R wave of 40 makes 85, well over 35.

cards.t: Right versus left ventricular hypertrophy compared
k: R greater than S versus deep S
q: how do right and left ventricular hypertrophy differ on an ECG
which leads show deep S waves
what is the axis in right versus left ventricular hypertrophy
cards.x:
Right and left ventricular hypertrophy pull the picture in opposite directions.

- V1 (the chest lead just right of the sternum) and V2 (the next lead to the left): right shows more R than S; left shows deep S waves.
- Lateral leads: left shows tall R waves in I, aVL, V5 (fifth chest lead) and V6 (sixth chest lead), along with lateral T inversion.
- Axis: right shows right axis deviation (supportive); left may show left axis deviation.
- Criteria: right is an R to S ratio of 1 or more in V1 and V2. Left is S in V1 or V2 plus R in V5 or V6 of 35 millimeters or more, R in aVL over 12, or any chest lead over 45.

Right is supported by right atrial enlargement, right axis deviation and strain, and the criterion is unreliable with right bundle branch block, posterior infarction or age under 7 or 8.

cards.t: Left ventricular hypertrophy as an infarction mimic
q: what conditions mimic ST-elevation myocardial infarction
why does left ventricular hypertrophy look like a heart attack
what is the most common mimic of infarction
cards.x:
Several conditions can raise the ST segment without being an infarction. The mimics of ST-elevation myocardial infarction are left ventricular hypertrophy, pericarditis, benign early repolarization, Brugada syndrome, left bundle branch block and ventricular paced rhythms, and hypothermia.

Left ventricular hypertrophy is known as the most common mimic. A thickened left ventricle alters repolarization, which changes the ST segment and T wave. The picture is ST elevation in V1 (first chest lead) to V3 (third chest lead) that is concave, curving upward. It comes with T wave inversion in the lateral leads.

cards.t: Why a bundle branch block widens the QRS
q: why does a bundle branch block make the QRS wide
why is there a notch in the QRS in bundle branch block
why do you lose the Q wave in left bundle branch block
cards.x:
A bundle branch block makes the QRS (the spike made by the ventricles) wide because one ventricle has to fire late.

Take left bundle branch block, a total failure of the left bundle. Impulses from the His bundle travel down the right bundle normally, so the right ventricle contracts first. The left ventricle then depends on myocyte-to-myocyte transmission across the heart, which is much slower than the normal conduction pathway. Its contraction is delayed, so the QRS is wide. Because the ventricles contract in sequence instead of together, the QRS shows two complexes, the double QRS phenomenon. And because the septal fascicle is blocked, the septal Q wave is lost, which is why there are no Q waves in the lateral leads.

Right bundle branch block is the mirror image: the left ventricle contracts normally, the right ventricle waits for slow muscle-to-muscle spread, and the same delay widens the QRS.

cards.t: Left anterior and left posterior fascicular blocks (hemiblocks)
q: what is a left anterior fascicular block
how is a left posterior fascicular block different
which fascicular block is more common
cards.x:
The left bundle splits into fascicles, so a block can hit just one of them. These are called hemiblocks.

- Left anterior fascicular block (left anterior hemiblock): the left anterior fascicle fails. The axis swings left: lead I mostly positive and aVF mostly negative. Look for a small q in lead I and a small r in lead III, with leads II and III mostly negative. The QRS (the spike made by the ventricles) stays narrow. It is the most common intraventricular conduction abnormality during an acute myocardial infarction.
- Left posterior fascicular block (left posterior hemiblock): the left posterior fascicle fails. The axis swings right: lead I mostly negative and aVF mostly positive, with an r in lead I and a q in lead III. It is far less common than the anterior block.

cards.t: Chamber enlargement versus ventricular hypertrophy
q: what is the difference between chamber enlargement and hypertrophy
what causes atrial enlargement
does hypertrophy make the ventricle bigger or smaller inside
cards.x:
These two sound alike but are different problems:

- Chamber enlargement is stretching of the chamber, which causes dilation. It is seen most in the atria, due to valve disease and regurgitation (leaking valves), pulmonary hypertension, lung disease such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and pulmonary embolism.
- Ventricular hypertrophy is actual enlargement and thickening of the cardiac muscle. In pressure overload the thick wall can take up room and make the chamber smaller, but in volume overload the chamber dilates as well.

A useful picture: enlargement is a chamber stretched out like an inflated balloon, while hypertrophy is a wall that has bulked up, which in the classic pressure-overload form squeezes its own cavity.

cards.t: The coronary arteries and the areas each one supplies
q: what does the right coronary artery supply
what does the left anterior descending artery supply
which artery supplies the lateral wall
cards.x:
