Four arteries matter. The left coronary artery (the left main) leaves the aorta and divides into two branches, the circumflex and the left anterior descending. The right coronary artery leaves the aorta on its own. Each one has its own territory, which is why the wall that is affected points to the artery that is blocked.

- Right coronary artery: the right atrium, the right ventricle, the bottom of the left ventricle and the back of the septum. A blockage causes inferior infarction, sometimes with right ventricular involvement. It supplies the inferior wall in about 80 to 85 percent of people.
- Left anterior descending artery: the front (and bottom) of the left ventricle and the front of the septum. A blockage causes septal, anterior or anteroseptal infarction.
- Circumflex artery: the left atrium and the side and back of the left ventricle. A blockage causes lateral, high lateral or posterior infarction.

The coronary veins carry used, oxygen-poor blood back to the right atrium. They are not the vessels that block.

cards.t: Matching the wall to the artery, and the left main
q: how do I match an infarction wall to its artery
what happens when the left main is blocked
what artery causes a high lateral infarction
cards.x:
Here is the matching, wall to artery:

- Inferior goes with the right coronary artery.
- Septal, anterior and anteroseptal go with the left anterior descending artery.
- Lateral, high lateral and posterior go with the circumflex.
- Right ventricle goes with the right coronary artery.

The left main is the special case, because it feeds both the left anterior descending and the circumflex. So a blockage high enough to raise the ST segment across the septal, anterior and lateral leads together is usually in one of two places. One is the proximal left anterior descending artery. The other is the left main split.

A high lateral infarction alone, in leads I and aVL, points to an isolated circumflex blockage. However, a diagonal branch of the left anterior descending artery can also supply that wall. So I and aVL alone do not rule out the left anterior descending artery.

cards.t: The J point, ST elevation, ST depression and the baseline
q: what is the J point
how do you measure ST elevation or depression
why use the TP segment instead of the PR segment as baseline
cards.x:
The J point is the junction between the QRS (the spike made by the ventricles) and the ST segment. The ST segment starts at the J point and ends where the T wave begins. In a healthy heart both the J point and the ST segment sit at baseline.

Cardiac events such as myocardial ischemia (reduced blood flow to heart muscle) can push the J point above or below that baseline. Above is ST elevation and below is ST depression, and the distance from the J point to the baseline is the amount of deviation.

To judge it, compare the J point with the TP (T-to-P) segment, the resting stretch between beats. At fast rates the TP segment can be hard to find, so compare the J point with the beginning of the QRS instead. Avoid the PR segment as a baseline when you can, because the atria are still active then; the TP segment is the moment of complete rest.

cards.t: Hyperacute T waves: the first sign of ischemia
q: what are hyperacute T waves
how are hyperacute T waves different from normal T waves
why are hyperacute T waves easy to miss
cards.x:
Hyperacute T waves are often the very first sign of cardiac ischemia. They are broad, higher than usual and symmetrical, meaning both sides of the hill look alike.

That shape is the clue, because a normal T wave is asymmetrical: a slow initial upstroke followed by a sharper negative terminal fall, at a modest height.

They are easy to miss because nothing has been raised yet. There is no ST elevation, so there is nothing obvious to call. Tall, symmetrical T waves are the thing to look for.

cards.t: ST depression and subendocardial ischemia
q: why does subendocardial ischemia cause ST depression
what does global ST depression mean
which layer of the heart is the subendocardium
cards.x:
Subendocardial ischemia is a lack of blood flow limited to the innermost layer of the wall. The coronary arteries run on the outer, epicardial surface, so the inner layer is the part that goes short. The electrode facing that wall then records ST segment depression.

The typical picture is widespread ST depression, often most obvious in the lateral chest leads and often with elevation in aVR. So when the ST segment is pushed below baseline across the whole tracing, think subendocardial ischemia, the inside layer only.

cards.t: ST elevation and transmural ischemia (injury)
q: why does transmural ischemia cause ST elevation
what does ST elevation in V1 to V4 mean
what is the difference between subendocardial and transmural ischemia
cards.x:
Transmural ischemia, also called injury, means the lack of blood flow now spans the full thickness of the wall instead of just the inner layer. The electrode facing that wall records ST segment elevation: the J point sits above the baseline.

The contrast with subendocardial ischemia is how deep it goes. Inner layer only gives ST depression. The full wall gives ST elevation.

An example is ST elevation with broad, tall hyperacute T waves in the front chest leads, V1 (first chest lead) to V4 (fourth chest lead). That is transmural ischemia in the anteroseptal territory. The left anterior descending artery supplies that territory.

cards.t: T-wave inversion
q: what does T wave inversion mean
how is T wave inversion different from hyperacute T waves
when does T wave inversion appear in ischemia
cards.x:
T-wave inversion is a sign of ischemia. It is the latest of the T-wave signs, coming after hyperacute T waves. When it appears together with active ST elevation, it means one of two things: the event is progressing, or reperfusion has occurred (blood flow has returned).

A quick way to keep it separate from hyperacute T waves: inverted T waves point below the baseline, while hyperacute T waves are upright, tall and broad.

cards.t: Pathologic Q waves and infarction
q: what makes a Q wave pathologic
what do pathologic Q waves mean
what is a QS complex
cards.x:
Pathologic Q waves usually mean infarction, which is the actual death of heart tissue, from either a previous or an acute event. A Q wave counts as pathologic when it is:

- longer than 0.04 seconds (one small box), and
- deeper than 2 millimeters (two small boxes), or, when there is an R wave, deeper than 25 percent of the R wave's height.

Why does dead tissue make a deep Q wave? Dead tissue under an electrode cannot depolarize. So the electrode sees current moving away from it and records a deep first negative deflection.

If there is no R wave at all, the single negative deflection is technically a QS (single negative deflection) complex. In the setting of an infarction it is read as a pathologic Q wave. Q waves in a patient with no reported heart history point to a previous infarction the patient did not know about.

cards.t: Ischemia, injury and infarction side by side
k: ST depression vs elevation vs Q waves
q: what is the difference between ischemia, injury and infarction
which ECG finding goes with which stage
which layer of the heart wall is involved in each
cards.x:
Ischemia, injury and infarction are three levels of trouble from poor blood flow to heart muscle, and each has its own matching finding on the electrocardiogram (ECG). Keep the pairings straight:

- Hyperacute T waves (broad, tall, symmetrical): ischemia, often the very first sign, when the event is just starting.
- ST depression, often global: subendocardial ischemia, which involves the innermost layer of the wall.
- ST elevation in contiguous leads: transmural ischemia, also called injury, which involves the full thickness of the wall. Injury in progress.
- Pathologic Q waves: infarction, which is death of tissue in the dead area. They come from a previous or an acute event.
- Inverted T waves: ischemia, a later sign.

The rule: ST depression goes with subendocardial ischemia, ST elevation with transmural injury, Q waves with dead tissue and hyperacute T waves with the first minutes. A pairing of ST depression with transmural injury, or Q waves with reversible ischemia, is wrong.

cards.t: Which leads look at which wall, and reciprocal leads
k: septal anterior lateral inferior posterior leads
q: which leads show an inferior infarction
what are reciprocal changes
why does the anterior wall have no reciprocal leads
cards.x:
Leads are contiguous when they look at the same region, such as II, III and aVF, or I and aVL. Reciprocal changes are the mirror image of a cardiac event, showing up on the opposite leads, which look at the same area from the other side.

- Septal: V1 (first chest lead) and V2 (second chest lead). No reciprocal leads. Left anterior descending artery.
- Anterior: V3 (third chest lead) and V4 (fourth chest lead). No reciprocal leads. Left anterior descending artery.
- Lateral: I, aVL, V5 (fifth chest lead) and V6 (sixth chest lead). Reciprocal in II, III and aVF. Circumflex.
- Inferior: II, III and aVF. Reciprocal in I and aVL. Right coronary artery.
- Posterior: none on the standard 12-lead; the reciprocal change is in V1 to V4. Circumflex.

The anterior walls have no reciprocal leads because no standard lead looks at the back of the heart. The most common reciprocal pair on the standard 12-lead is lead III and lead aVL.

cards.t: Reciprocal changes (the mirror image on opposite leads)
q: what are reciprocal changes
which leads are reciprocal to the inferior leads
why do some walls have no reciprocal leads
cards.x:
Reciprocal changes are the mirror image of a cardiac event, showing up on the opposite leads, which look at the same area of the heart from the other side. So when one wall shows ST elevation, the leads facing it from across the heart show ST depression.

The pairs are:

- Inferior wall (II, III and aVF): reciprocal changes in I and aVL.
- Lateral and anterolateral walls: reciprocal changes in II, III and aVF.
- Posterior wall: nothing faces it on the standard tracing, and its reciprocal change appears in the front chest leads, V1 (first chest lead) to V4 (fourth chest lead).
- Septal, anterior and anteroseptal walls: no direct reciprocal leads (inferior ST depression sometimes appears).

The reason is that no standard lead looks at the back of the heart. The first two chest leads look mostly at the septum, and every other lead looks at the left ventricle. The most common reciprocal pair on the standard 12-lead is lead III and lead aVL.

cards.t: ST-elevation myocardial infarction criteria and reciprocal changes
q: what are the criteria for ST-elevation myocardial infarction
what is a reciprocal change
does absence of reciprocal changes rule out ischemia
cards.x:
An ST segment elevation myocardial infarction is considered when there is 1 millimeter of elevation or more in 2 or more contiguous leads. This can be with or without reciprocal changes. In V2 (second chest lead) and V3 (third chest lead) the threshold is higher.

ST depression should be considered a reciprocal change until proven otherwise if ST elevation also exists on the same tracing. Reciprocal changes are a confirmatory sign of cardiac ischemia when ST elevation is present. But their absence does not exclude ischemia, so you cannot rule it out just because the mirror image is missing.

cards.t: Inferior, high lateral and anteroseptal infarction patterns
q: what does an inferior infarction look like on the ECG
what leads show a high lateral infarction
what leads show an anteroseptal infarction
cards.x:
Three classic patterns, each with the leads that rise and the leads that mirror them:

- Inferior: ST elevation in II, III and aVF. Reciprocal depression in I and aVL. Most often the right coronary artery.
- High lateral: elevation in I and aVL. Reciprocal depression in the inferior leads III and aVF. I and aVL carry the elevation that localizes it. The circumflex supplies the side of the left ventricle, and a diagonal branch of the left anterior descending can also cause this pattern.
- Anteroseptal: elevation in V1 (first chest lead), V2 (second chest lead) and V3 (third chest lead), looking at the anterior and septal walls. Left anterior descending artery. On its own it has no reciprocal leads.

Contiguous leads that rise together point to the wall that is involved.

cards.t: Posterior infarction and the V7 to V9 back leads
q: how do you recognize a posterior infarction
where are leads V7 to V9 placed
what does isolated ST depression in V1 to V4 mean
cards.x:
Isolated posterior wall infarctions are 3 to 4 percent of all acute myocardial infarctions. They are typically from a blocked or narrowed circumflex artery. The standard tracing does not look at the back of the heart, so the clue is indirect.

The clue is isolated ST depression in the front chest leads, V1 (first chest lead) to V4 (fourth chest lead), with no ST elevation anywhere. This should always be considered a reciprocal (mirror-image) change for a posterior infarction until proven otherwise. A posterior tracing must then be obtained.

To get it, move V4, V5 (fifth chest lead) and V6 (sixth chest lead) to the back and relabel them V7 (seventh chest lead), V8 (eighth chest lead) and V9 (ninth chest lead). Then repeat the tracing. This is at times called a 15-lead electrocardiogram. V7 goes at the posterior axillary line, V8 at the tip of the scapula and V9 between the scapula and the spine, all at the same level. ST elevation in V7 to V9 confirms a posterior wall infarction.

cards.t: Inferior infarction with right ventricular involvement and the V4R lead
k: hypotension clear lungs jugular vein distension
q: how do I know if an inferior infarction involves the right ventricle
where is V4R placed
what symptoms suggest right ventricular involvement
cards.x:
Inferior infarctions caused by the right coronary artery can involve the right ventricle too. Suspect it whenever a patient with acute coronary syndrome symptoms has all three of these together: hypotension (low blood pressure), clear lung sounds and jugular vein distension (swollen neck veins). More ST elevation in III than in II already raises suspicion.

To rule it in or out, move V4 (the fourth chest lead) to the right side of the chest. Put it in the fifth intercostal space at the midclavicular line, a mirror image of its normal spot. Then repeat the tracing. The lead is then marked V4R (the right-sided fourth chest lead). Elevation in V4R confirms right ventricular involvement.

Summary of the extra tracing to order: isolated ST depression in the front chest leads points to the back leads. Inferior elevation with low blood pressure, clear lungs and distended neck veins points to V4R.

cards.t: Why the innermost layer of the heart wall starves first
q: why does ischemia hit the inner layer first
how do the coronary arteries run through the wall
what happens to blood supply past a narrowing
cards.x:
The coronary arteries run on the outer surface of the heart, the epicardium, and then dive inward, getting smaller as they go. The innermost layer, the endocardium, is the last stop on the way.

Past a narrowing, there is less blood to share. The epicardium, being closest to the artery, takes what there is, and the endocardium gets what is left. That is why the inner layer starves first, and why subendocardial ischemia shows on the tracing as ST depression.

cards.t: Plaque, stable angina and why pain persists at rest
q: what causes most ischemic heart disease
what is stable angina
what happens when a plaque ruptures
cards.x:
Atherosclerotic plaque, a fatty buildup in the artery wall, causes most ischemic heart disease.

Stable angina is pain that comes with a predictable amount of exertion and is relieved within about 20 minutes of rest.

The picture changes when a plaque ruptures. Platelets, the small cells that clump to form clots, aggregate on it, the narrowing worsens, and the pain persists at rest.

cards.t: Why ischemia moves the baseline and why Q waves form
k: R wave fades as cells die
q: why does ischemia cause ST depression and elevation
why does the sodium-potassium pump matter in ischemia
why does the R wave shrink in infarction
cards.x:
Without oxygen, cells cannot make adenosine triphosphate, their energy molecule. The sodium-potassium pump then fails and potassium leaks out. The neighboring cells rest at a less negative level than normal and depolarize early.

That early depolarization shifts the baseline, and which way depends on how deep it goes. If it is in the inner layer only, the current moves toward the lead and the baseline shifts up, so the ST segment looks depressed. If it spans the full wall, the current runs away from the lead and the ST segment looks elevated.

When cells actually die, they can no longer depolarize, so the R wave shrinks toward a Q wave.

cards.t: Acute pericarditis on the tracing
q: what does acute pericarditis look like on an ECG
why does pericarditis change the PR segment
how do I tell pericarditis from a heart attack
cards.x:
Pericarditis is inflammation of the pericardium, the two-layered sac around the heart. The whole pericardium is inflamed, including the part over the atria. That is why the PR segment changes as well as the ST segment.

The tracing shows:

- PR depression, and PR elevation in aVR.
- Global, concave ST elevation, meaning it is in many leads and curves upward like a bowl.
- No reciprocal ST depression anywhere on the tracing, except in aVR and V1 (the first chest lead).

The last point is the key separator from a heart attack. If there is ST depression in any lead other than aVR and V1, or any new Q wave, it is not typical pericarditis. An acute ST-elevation infarction must be considered.

cards.t: Benign early repolarization
q: what is benign early repolarization
what is a J wave
is early repolarization dangerous
cards.x:
Benign early repolarization is also known as normal variant ST elevation. It is seen mostly in young men and has no clinical significance, which is the whole point of recognizing it: it looks worrying but is harmless.

The tracing shows:

- Terminal QRS (the spike made by the ventricles) notching, called the J wave, also known as the fishhook sign or Osborn wave. It is a notch at the end of the QRS where it meets the ST segment.
- Large T waves, sometimes symmetrical.
- No reciprocal ST depression outside aVR and V1 (the first chest lead).
- Unlike pericarditis, no PR segment depression.

cards.t: Causes of a prolonged QT interval
q: what causes a long QT interval
how do I judge QT prolongation
which drugs and conditions lengthen the QT
cards.x:
A long QT interval is not one disease with one picture, and it can turn up with things like these:

- Hypocalcemia (low calcium): a long ST segment lengthens the corrected QT (QTc).
- Hypothyroidism (underactive thyroid): prolonged QTc.
- Amiodarone: it slows phase 3 of the action potential.
- Tricyclic antidepressant overdose.

When judging prolongation, use the QTc, the QT corrected for heart rate, which the machine prints next to the raw QT. That correction is what stops a slow or fast heart rate from fooling you.

cards.t: Early repolarization versus pericarditis versus infarction
q: how do I tell pericarditis from early repolarization from infarction
which cause of ST elevation is localized
what rules out pericarditis
cards.x:
All three can raise the ST segment, so compare them across a few features.

- Infarction: localized to contiguous leads. ST shape convex or straight. Reciprocal depression expected (it confirms, but is not required). Q waves may be present.
- Pericarditis: global (many leads). ST shape concave. No reciprocal depression outside aVR and V1 (first chest lead). PR segment depressed, and elevated in aVR. A new Q wave points away from it.
- Early repolarization: global. Concave. No reciprocal depression outside aVR and V1. PR segment not depressed. Other clues: a J-point notch, large T waves and young men.

In short: infarction is local, with reciprocal changes expected but not required. The other two are global, with no reciprocal depression outside aVR and V1. The PR segment separates those two.

cards.t: The lead V6 ST/T ratio for pericarditis versus early repolarization
q: how do I use V6 to tell pericarditis from early repolarization
what is the 25 percent rule
how do I measure the ST to T ratio
cards.x:
When pericarditis and early repolarization are hard to tell apart, look at lead V6 (the sixth chest lead). Measure the height of the ST elevation, from the end of the PR segment to the J point, and compare it with the T wave's height.

- ST/T ratio above 25 percent: suggests pericarditis.
- ST/T ratio below 25 percent: suggests benign early repolarization.

Put simply, early repolarization has relatively more T wave and pericarditis has relatively more ST elevation. In an early repolarization example the ST height is well under a quarter of the T wave, while in a pericarditis example it is about half.

cards.t: Brugada syndrome
q: what is Brugada syndrome
what does Brugada look like on an ECG
what is the difference between type 1 and type 2 Brugada
cards.x:
Brugada syndrome is an inherited arrhythmogenic disease, meaning it is passed down and prone to causing rhythm problems. It affects the sodium channels of the right ventricular outflow tract and is most commonly seen in young men of Southeast Asian descent. These patients are at greater risk of lethal dysrhythmias such as polymorphic ventricular tachycardia and ventricular fibrillation.

There are two main patterns, and both are isolated to V1 (first chest lead) through V3 (third chest lead):

- Type 1: convex, coved-shaped ST elevation.
- Type 2: saddle-shaped (saddleback) ST elevation, which is also called the carousel horses sign.

On a tracing, think of Brugada when ST elevation like this is confined to V1 through V3.

cards.t: Sgarbossa's criteria and infarction in left bundle branch block
k: infarction in left bundle branch block
q: what are Sgarbossa's criteria
what does concordant mean
how do I diagnose infarction in left bundle branch block
cards.x:
Left bundle branch blocks and ventricular paced rhythms cause a wide QRS (the spike made by the ventricles). They also cause ST and T wave changes that point opposite to the QRS, often ST elevation in the right chest leads. Both make an ST-elevation infarction hard to locate.

Sgarbossa's criteria are used to diagnose an acute myocardial infarction in the presence of a left bundle branch block or a ventricularly paced rhythm. The first two are enough on their own. The third counts for less and is not enough alone:

- Concordant ST elevation of 1 millimeter or more in any lead with a positive QRS.
- Concordant ST depression of 1 millimeter or more in V1 (the first chest lead) to V3 (the third).
- Discordant ST elevation of 5 millimeters or more in any lead with a negative QRS.

Concordant means the ST change is on the same side of the baseline as the QRS. Discordant means the opposite side. Some discordance is normal in these blocks, which is why discordant elevation has to reach 5 millimeters to count.

cards.t: Hyperkalemia: peaked T waves to sine wave
q: what does hyperkalemia look like on an ECG
what is the order of ECG changes in hyperkalemia
what is a sine wave rhythm
cards.x:
Hyperkalemia means high potassium in the blood. It can cause a host of changes, including slow rhythms, fast rhythms, ST elevation, T wave abnormalities and atrioventricular and bundle branch blocks. But the classic signs show up in a set order as it worsens:

- Peaked, symmetric T waves: the early sign.
- Flattened P waves.
- A sine wave: the end stage.

In the late picture the QRS (the spike made by the ventricles) becomes very wide, the P waves vanish and everything slurs together into a sine-wave shape. Roughly, at about 6 milliequivalents per liter you see peaked T waves. Around 8 you see flat P waves, a long PR interval and a wide QRS. Above 9 you see a sine wave or asystole. Those values are approximate.

cards.t: Hypokalemia and U waves
q: what does hypokalemia look like on an ECG
what is a U wave
why does low potassium cause U waves
cards.x:
Hypokalemia is a serum potassium below 3.5 milliequivalents per liter. It prolongs repolarization, so its early signs are changes to the ST segment, the T wave and the U wave. A U wave is a small wave after the T wave, and prominent U waves with T wave flattening are classic signs.

The classic list is:

- T wave flattening.
- Prominent U waves.
- Fusion of an inverted T wave with the U wave.
- Prominent P waves.
- ST depression, with ST elevation in aVR.

The quick memory line: low potassium flattens the T wave and raises a U wave.

cards.t: Hypocalcemia and hypercalcemia: effects on the ST segment and QTc
q: what does hypocalcemia do to the ECG
what does hypercalcemia do to the ECG
why does calcium change the ST segment
cards.x:
Calcium acts on phase 2 of the action potential, the plateau. The ST segment is the part of the tracing that reflects it. So calcium changes move the ST segment.

- Hypocalcemia (low calcium) prolongs phase 2. That lengthens the ST segment without affecting the duration of the T wave. A longer ST segment means a prolonged QTc (the Q-to-T interval corrected for heart rate). Findings: prolonged QTc, T waves with normal shape, prolonged ST segment.
- Hypercalcemia (high calcium) shortens phase 2, shortening the ST segment. So the QTc shortens, and at times the T wave is pushed right against the QRS (the spike made by the ventricles). Findings: shortened QTc, T waves close to or attached to the end of the QRS, shortened ST segment.

cards.t: Potassium and calcium patterns side by side
q: how do I tell potassium changes from calcium changes on an ECG
what do sodium changes do to the tracing
what is the memory rule for electrolytes
cards.x:
One rule sums up the electrolyte changes: potassium moves the T wave, calcium moves the ST segment.

- High potassium (hyperkalemia): peaked, symmetric T waves; later flat P waves, a wide QRS (the spike made by the ventricles) and a sine wave.
- Low potassium (hypokalemia): flattened T waves and a prominent U wave, with ST depression. Repolarization is prolonged.
- Low calcium (hypocalcemia): a long ST segment before a normal T wave, and a prolonged QTc. Phase 2 is prolonged.
- High calcium (hypercalcemia): the T wave sits against the QRS, with a short ST segment and a shortened QTc. Phase 2 is shortened.

Sodium changes are not expected to change the tracing or the rhythm.

cards.t: Pulmonary embolism on the ECG (S1Q3T3)
q: what does a pulmonary embolism look like on an ECG
what is S1Q3T3
why does pulmonary embolism cause tachycardia
cards.x:
A pulmonary embolism (a clot in the lung's arteries) can show up on the tracing in several ways, each with its own reason:

- Tachycardia, from sympathetic nervous system activation by hypoxia (low oxygen).
- A more rightward axis, from dilation and enlargement of the right ventricle under high pressure.
- ST segment and T wave changes, from localized myocardial ischemia.
- The S1Q3T3 (S one, Q three, T three) pattern: a deep S wave in lead I, a Q wave in lead III and an inverted T wave in lead III.

A classic strip shows sinus tachycardia together with S1Q3T3.

cards.t: Hypothermia and Osborn waves
q: what does hypothermia look like on an ECG
what is an Osborn wave
what temperature causes Osborn waves
cards.x:
In hypothermia the ECG (electrocardiogram) changes follow the falling body temperature. As it approaches 35 degrees Celsius (95 degrees Fahrenheit), sinus bradycardia occurs, typically followed by prolongation of the intervals. Below 32 degrees Celsius (90 degrees Fahrenheit), Osborn waves become apparent. An Osborn wave, also called a J wave, is a notch at the end of the QRS (the spike made by the ventricles).

The trap is that Osborn waves are frequently mistaken for an ST elevation infarction. So a notch after the QRS across many leads, together with long intervals and a slow rhythm, can be hypothermia rather than an infarction.

cards.t: Digoxin toxicity on the tracing
q: what does digoxin toxicity do to the ECG
why does digoxin cause abnormal rhythms
what is the most common ECG abnormality in digoxin toxicity
cards.x:
Digoxin toxicity occurs when too much digoxin builds up in the body or when the heart becomes overly sensitive to it. Digoxin inhibits the sodium-potassium pump, which causes abnormal cell excitability, meaning heart cells fire when they should not.

The most common abnormality is frequent premature ventricular complexes. A classic strip shows ventricular bigeminy: a normal beat, then a premature ventricular complex, repeating every other beat.

cards.t: Amiodarone and tricyclic antidepressant effects on the tracing
q: what does amiodarone do to the ECG
what does a tricyclic antidepressant overdose look like on an ECG
why does a tricyclic antidepressant overdose widen the QRS
cards.x:
Two drugs can lengthen the QT interval through different channel effects.

- Amiodarone blocks sodium, potassium and calcium channels and acts as a beta blocker in the heart. It reduces conduction velocity, slows phase 3, suppresses sinoatrial automaticity and slows atrioventricular conduction. On the tracing that shows as QT prolongation and slowing of the heart rate and atrioventricular conduction.
- Tricyclic antidepressant overdose (for example amitriptyline) causes fast sodium-channel blockade, with a delay in potassium outflow, plus anticholinergic activity. It shows as QT prolongation and tachycardia (from the anticholinergic effect). The widened QRS (the spike made by the ventricles) is the sodium-channel effect.

cards.t: Why a paced rhythm can hide an infarction
q: what does a ventricular paced rhythm look like on a 12-lead
what is a pacing artifact
can a paced rhythm hide an infarction
cards.x:
A ventricular paced rhythm is a mimic: it can make a tracing look like an infarction or hide a real one. It has a recognizable look. A sharp vertical pacing spike, the pacing artifact, appears before each beat, followed by a wide QRS (the spike made by the ventricles). The T waves are contralateral, or discordant, meaning they point opposite the QRS, and there is often global ST elevation.

Like a left bundle branch block, a paced rhythm hides an infarction, so Sgarbossa's criteria are used to look for one.

cards.t: Preexcitation and Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome
q: what is Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome
what is a delta wave
what is the triad of Wolff-Parkinson-White
cards.x:
Preexcitation means the ventricles are activated earlier than normal, because a supraventricular impulse reaches them through an extra route. Normally the impulse must pass through the atrioventricular node, where it is slowed, before it reaches the His-Purkinje network. In preexcitation, an accessory pathway connects the atria to the ventricles and bypasses the atrioventricular node. The most common preexcitation syndrome is Wolff-Parkinson-White, and its accessory pathway is the Kent bundle.

The diagnostic triad is a short PR interval, a wide QRS (the spike made by the ventricles) and a delta wave.

- Short PR: the pathway bypasses the node, so the impulse arrives early.
- Delta wave: a slurring of the upstroke of the QRS. The bypassing impulse starts depolarizing the ventricles early, and once the normal impulse reaches the His-Purkinje network, the rest of the QRS looks normal.

Type A has a left-sided Kent bundle and a QRS mostly positive in V1 (first chest lead). Type B has a right-sided one and a QRS mostly negative in V1.

cards.t: Orthodromic and antidromic reentrant tachycardia in preexcitation
q: what is orthodromic versus antidromic tachycardia
why is antidromic tachycardia wide
how does an accessory pathway cause a tachycardia
cards.x:
In a person with an accessory pathway, the pathway and the normal pathway can form a reentry circuit, a loop that keeps a tachycardia going. A premature atrial or ventricular complex near the accessory pathway can start premature depolarization and set the loop off. Which way the loop runs decides the look:

- Orthodromic: down the normal pathway, toward the ventricles, and back up the accessory pathway. This makes a regular, narrow-complex tachycardia.
- Antidromic: down the accessory pathway and back up the normal pathway, toward the atria. This makes a regular, monomorphic, wide tachycardia. Because the ventricles are activated entirely through the accessory pathway, the QRS is wide and can look like ventricular tachycardia.

At times it is impossible to tell orthodromic reentry from supraventricular tachycardia, or antidromic reentry from ventricular tachycardia, on the tracing alone. History helps if the patient knows of the pathway.

cards.t: Hyperthyroidism and hypothyroidism on the ECG
q: what does hyperthyroidism do to the ECG
what does hypothyroidism do to the ECG
what is the most common rhythm in hyperthyroidism
cards.x:
The thyroid sets the body's pace, and the heart follows it.

- Hyperthyroidism is a state of adrenergic hyperactivity, meaning the body's adrenaline-type signaling is turned up. Sinus tachycardia is the most commonly observed finding. Atrial fibrillation is the second most common.
- Hypothyroidism slows the metabolic rate and myocardial contractility. The tracing shows sinus bradycardia, a global low-voltage QRS (the spike made by the ventricles), flattened or inverted T waves, a prolonged QTc (the Q-to-T interval corrected for heart rate) and low-amplitude P waves.

So an overactive thyroid means fast rhythms, and an underactive thyroid means a slow rhythm with small, flat waves.
